briefing.text: SCLC subtypes SCLC-A, SCLC-N and SCLC-P are defined by RNA or protein (IHC) expression of the transcription factors ASCL1, NEUROD1 and POU2F3, not by any DNA mutation or copy-number change. Before choosing a label, list every file and column provided and search them (case-insensitive) for mRNA expression, IHC scores or a subtype annotation (ascl1, neurod, pou2f3, subtype). If such a variable exists, call subtypes per sample with a relative-expression rule (highest of the TFs) and report mixed ASCL1/NEUROD1 calls rather than forcing absence.
briefing.reason: Whether a subtype-defining variable exists in the tables is the deciding question for which label the task rules allow; teams must check for it explicitly rather than infer subtype from genomic tables.

briefing.text: ASCL1, NEUROD1 and POU2F3 may not be on the targeted sequencing panel used here; check whether they appear in data_cna.txt, the Hugo_Symbol column of data_mutations.txt and the panel in data_gene_panel_matrix.txt. A gene missing from these tables means it was not measured, not that the subtype is absent.
briefing.reason: Prevents misreading missing measurement as a negative result about subtype presence.

briefing.text: MYC-family amplification (MYCL, MYC, MYCN) is only loosely associated with SCLC subtypes, and most SCLCs carry none, so CNA cannot assign or exclude a subtype for a sample. If tabulated, treat it as indirect context only, not as grounds for a True/False label.
briefing.reason: Stops teams from using a weak genomic proxy as if it measured subtype.

briefing.text: The cohort mixes PDX model samples and patient tumour samples (see SAMPLE_CLASS in data_clinical_sample.txt), and SAMPLE_TYPE values differ in case (e.g. Metastasis/metastasis). The hypothesis concerns PDX/CDX models only: filter by SAMPLE_CLASS and normalise case before counting anything.
briefing.reason: Any analysis must be restricted to the model samples the hypothesis is about.

briefing.text: Decide the label strictly from what the given tables contain, following the task's label definitions; do not use published knowledge about SCLC models to assign a label the data themselves do not support.
briefing.reason: Keeps the judgement grounded in the data rather than prior beliefs about the literature.

shared_assumptions: Both teams assumed that an SCLC transcriptional subtype can only be assigned from RNA/IHC of ASCL1/NEUROD1/POU2F3, and that the absence of those genes from the DNA panel tables means no variable is relevant. Neither team checked whether any genomic correlate in the given tables is treated as subtype-informative (for example, which panel genes are and are not measured), or wrote down why such a proxy is ruled out.

Both treated every SAMPLE_CLASS=PDX row as one group of 'PDX/CDX models'. Neither separated circulating-tumour-cell-derived models from tissue-derived ones, and neither checked histology (CANCER_TYPE_DETAILED), even though some samples are not classic SCLC.
unused_evidence: PROCEDURE_TYPE='Blood Draw' and TISSUE_SITE='Blood/blood' mark about 8 PDX rows that are in effect CDX models. These are the only way the data can tell CDX from PDX, and neither team used them to check that both model types the hypothesis names are present.

CANCER_TYPE_DETAILED / ONCOTREE_CODE include combined SCLC, LCNEC and lung neuroendocrine tumour samples. Neither team tabulated these within the PDX class. Their sole label is unlikely to change, but they define who is in scope.
The patient-tumour (SAMPLE_CLASS=Tumor) samples and the PDX_SAMPLE_DAYS_FROM_DIAGNOSIS column were not used. They could only ever support indirect comparisons, and neither team stated that.
unresolved_weak_points: Team A named indirect genomic evidence as its weakest point and settled it by judgement, without stating a rule. Team B named it and only reported it. Neither team showed that no DNA-level variable in the tables is a recognised subtype marker; they asserted it.

Neither team considered the asymmetry of a claim that something is 'not present'. They did not state explicitly whether being unable to detect a subtype counts as support (True) or as no information (Not verifiable).
second_readings: 'Not present in the PDX/CDX models' could mean that no model carries any of the three subtypes, or that the subtypes are not represented or annotated in the model collection. Under the second reading the absence of any subtype annotation might be argued to bear on the claim, although that reading confuses the data with biology.
'PDX/CDX models' could mean all xenograft rows, or require that CDX (blood-derived) models be identified separately. The scope differs, though neither scope yields subtype data.
challenge.verdict: I trust the agreed Not verifiable label highly. I checked the tables myself: none of ASCL1, NEUROD1 or POU2F3 is in the CNA or mutation tables, and there is no expression, IHC or subtype column, so the shared blind spots I found (CDX identification, histology scope, and an unstated rule for genomic proxies) are unlikely to change the label.

findings.question: Are SCLC molecular subtypes (ASCL1-, NEUROD1-, POU2F3-defined) ever assigned or reliably inferred from DNA-only targeted panel data (mutations or copy number) rather than from RNA or protein expression?
findings.answer: No. SCLC A/N/P subtypes are defined by transcription-factor expression, measured by RNA (NMF or relative TF expression: Rudin et al. 2019 Nat Rev Cancer; Gay et al. 2021 Cancer Cell) or by IHC (Park et al. 2024 eBioMedicine, where targeted DNA sequencing was only compared across IHC-defined subtypes). Chemi et al. 2022 (Nat Cancer) state that 'genomic profiling has not mapped to the TF-based SCLC subtypes', and a 2022 Sci Adv paper says large-scale sequencing has not supported stratifying SCLC by its genome. The DNA-based subtyping methods that do exist use DNA methylation (RRBS-based SCLC-DMC classifier; cfDNA methylome) or cfDNA chromatin and nucleosome signals at TF binding sites and transcription start sites (Hiatt et al. 2024 Sci Adv). None of them uses somatic mutations or copy number. MYC-family amplifications are enriched by subtype (MYCL with ASCL1; MYC with NEUROD1 and POU2F3; MYCN with NEUROD1), but only as loose associations, not as a subtype call. So a mutation, CNA, SV or segment table cannot be used as a validated proxy for A/N/P subtype.
findings.text: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: Are SCLC molecular subtypes (ASCL1-, NEUROD1-, POU2F3-defined) ever assigned or reliably inferred from DNA-only targeted panel data (mutations or copy number) rather than from RNA or protein expression? ANSWER: No. SCLC A/N/P subtypes are defined by transcription-factor expression, measured by RNA (NMF or relative TF expression: Rudin et al. 2019 Nat Rev Cancer; Gay et al. 2021 Cancer Cell) or by IHC (Park et al. 2024 eBioMedicine, where targeted DNA sequencing was only compared across IHC-defined subtypes). Chemi et al. 2022 (Nat Cancer) state that 'genomic profiling has not mapped to the TF-based SCLC subtypes', and a 2022 Sci Adv paper says large-scale sequencing has not supported stratifying SCLC by its genome. The DNA-based subtyping methods that do exist use DNA methylation (RRBS-based SCLC-DMC classifier; cfDNA methylome) or cfDNA chromatin and nucleosome signals at TF binding sites and transcription start sites (Hiatt et al. 2024 Sci Adv). None of them uses somatic mutations or copy number. MYC-family amplifications are enriched by subtype (MYCL with ASCL1; MYC with NEUROD1 and POU2F3; MYCN with NEUROD1), but only as loose associations, not as a subtype call. So a mutation, CNA, SV or segment table cannot be used as a validated proxy for A/N/P subtype. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://www.nature.com/articles/s43018-022-00415-9, https://www.science.org/doi/full/10.1126/sciadv.abp8674, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10982990/, https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.adk2082, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ebiom.2024.105062, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41568-019-0133-9, https://www.lungcancerjournal.info/article/S0169-5002(26)00733-6/pdf, https://aacrjournals.org/cancerrescommun/article/6/3/545/775222/Subclassification-of-Small-Cell-Lung-Cancer-Based.
